title: The Access Layer: Families, Dynasties and Continuity Networks
editorialBoundary: This dataset measures documented access, authority, voting control, appointment power and institutional continuity. It does not infer criminality, secret coordination or total control from a surname, marriage, wealth, philanthropy or social contact.
finalConclusion: The strongest documented family control is found where law or corporate governance explicitly preserves hereditary office, voting rights, board influence or foundation ownership. Royal dynasties can hold formal state authority. Corporate dynasties can preserve strategic control through voting shares, foundations and holding companies. The evidence does not show that one family or coordinated family bloc controls the monetary, security, regulatory, technological and financial systems of the world. Those systems are governed through overlapping offices, boards, member states, regulators, professional networks and capital structures. Families matter most where succession and control rights are legally embedded; elsewhere, access is real but fragmented, conditional and contestable.

families.name: House of Saud
documentedAccess: Saudi governance is legally monarchical and succession is limited to descendants of the founder King Abdulaziz.
The King directs state policy and senior appointments are made by royal order.
Senior members of the dynasty occupy central executive, energy, defence and state-governance positions.
constraints: International alliances, markets and security dependencies
Internal succession rules and royal-family bargaining
families.strongestCounterargument: Formal dynastic authority is exceptionally high, but that does not make the family autonomous from state bureaucracy, oil markets, domestic legitimacy, international security relationships or global financial infrastructure.
families.unsupportedClaim: The record does not establish that the House of Saud commands non-Saudi central banks, Western governments or a unified global system.

families.name: Al Nahyan family
documentedAccess: The ruler of Abu Dhabi sits on the UAE Federal Supreme Council, the federation's highest constitutional authority.
The UAE presidency is currently held by the ruler of Abu Dhabi, and substantive Supreme Council decisions require the votes of Abu Dhabi and Dubai.
Abu Dhabi retains extensive local jurisdiction and is the centre of major sovereign-capital and security institutions.
constraints: Federal bargaining with the six other emirates
Constitutional division between federal and emirate powers
Global energy, finance and alliance dependencies
Institutional management rather than personal direction of every asset
families.strongestCounterargument: The family has documented constitutional and capital access, but the UAE is a federation and major institutions retain professional management, legal mandates and external dependencies.
families.unsupportedClaim: The evidence does not show that every Abu Dhabi investment or UAE policy is personally directed by one family member or a single concealed command centre.

families.name: Al Maktoum family
documentedAccess: Dubai is a hereditary sheikhdom whose ruler sits on the Federal Supreme Council.
The ruler of Dubai is the UAE Vice President and Prime Minister.
Substantive federal decisions require a majority that includes both Abu Dhabi and Dubai.
constraints: Federal balance with Abu Dhabi and other emirates
Dependence on global logistics, tourism and finance
families.strongestCounterargument: Dubai's commercial reach is large, but its authority is constitutionally shared and its economic model is highly exposed to international markets and federal coordination.
families.unsupportedClaim: Commercial prominence and family rule do not establish command over global finance, media or technology systems.

families.name: Al Thani family
documentedAccess: Qatar's constitutional succession provisions establish hereditary rule within the Al Thani family.
The Amir is the head of state and succession is constitutionally structured.
The ruling structure has access to executive appointments, sovereign capital, energy strategy and foreign policy.
constraints: Small-state dependence on external security and markets
Professional management of sovereign and commercial entities
families.strongestCounterargument: The family's domestic authority is explicit, but Qatar's international leverage remains dependent on energy markets, alliances, host-state agreements and institutional execution.
families.unsupportedClaim: The record does not establish that Qatari investments or media relationships amount to control of foreign governments.

families.name: Wallenberg family and foundations
documentedAccess: The Wallenberg Foundations hold decisive voting influence in Investor AB, with the largest foundation alone holding more than 42 percent of votes as of June 2026.
The ecosystem states that the three largest foundations collectively hold 50 percent of Investor's votes.
Family members hold senior board positions while Investor uses board participation across a portfolio spanning finance, defence, industrials, pharmaceuticals and technology.
constraints: Swedish and EU law and regulation
families.strongestCounterargument: The ecosystem demonstrates exceptional corporate continuity and board access, but it is not equivalent to control of the Swedish state or every company in which Investor owns shares.
families.unsupportedClaim: The evidence does not support claims that the Wallenbergs secretly direct Sweden, NATO or European institutions as a unified private government.

families.name: Agnelli–Elkann descendants
documentedAccess: Giovanni Agnelli B.V., owned by descendants of Fiat founder Giovanni Agnelli, held 83.97 percent of Exor voting rights at 31 December 2025.
The stated purpose of the family vehicle is to preserve unity and continuity of its controlling interest in Exor.
Exor's portfolio creates board and capital access across automotive, luxury, healthcare, media and investment assets.
constraints: No direct authority over monetary or security systems
families.strongestCounterargument: The family has unusually clear voting control over Exor, but portfolio-company control varies by stake, governance agreement and jurisdiction.
families.unsupportedClaim: Exor control does not prove control of the Italian government, European regulators or all companies linked to the family.

families.name: Møller family foundations and holding structure
documentedAccess: A.P. Møller Holding held 52.50 percent of votes in A.P. Møller–Mærsk as of June 2026.
The family foundation and support foundation held additional substantial voting positions.
The structure preserves long-term influence over a company embedded in global shipping, ports and logistics.
families.strongestCounterargument: Voting control over Maersk is clear, but influence is concentrated in logistics rather than a comprehensive cross-system command structure.
families.unsupportedClaim: Control of a major shipping group does not establish control of world trade, ports owned by others or government policy.

families.name: Hoffmann–Oeri founding-family pool
documentedAccess: A shareholder group with pooled voting rights owned 64.97 percent of Roche's issued voting shares at the end of 2025.
Representatives of the family shareholder pool sit on Roche's board.
Roche publicly describes the founder-family shareholder structure as supporting long-term continuity.
constraints: Concentration mainly in one corporate group
families.strongestCounterargument: The voting pool has clear corporate control, but Roche's scientific, regulatory and commercial decisions remain institutionally constrained.
families.unsupportedClaim: Family voting control at Roche does not prove control over global medicine regulation, public-health agencies or healthcare systems.

families.name: Heineken family control structure
documentedAccess: L'Arche Green N.V., which anchors the Heineken control structure, is owned 88.98 percent by the Heineken family.
Heineken Holding states that its ownership structure exists to preserve continuity, independence and stability of the group.
The structure supports long-term family influence over one of the world's largest brewing groups.
families.strongestCounterargument: The family has a strong continuity structure, but its reach is commercial and sector-specific rather than systemic across finance, security or law.
families.unsupportedClaim: Control of a global consumer company does not amount to control of governments, media systems or public policy.

historicalArchitects.name: Rothschild banking houses
historicalArchitects.documentedHistory: Distinct Rothschild family banking houses played important roles in nineteenth-century sovereign finance, railways and cross-border capital markets.
historicalArchitects.presentAssessment: Modern Rothschild-branded businesses are separate regulated entities. Historical significance and family continuity justify investigation, but do not establish control of central banks, governments or a unified global financial system today.

historicalArchitects.name: Rockefeller family and philanthropic institutions
historicalArchitects.documentedHistory: Rockefeller wealth and foundations materially influenced twentieth-century philanthropy, education, medicine, public health and policy research.
historicalArchitects.presentAssessment: Institution-building influence is documented. Claims that the family currently commands the US government, global health system or all foundation networks require evidence that has not been established.

historicalArchitects.name: Warburg banking family
historicalArchitects.documentedHistory: Members of the Warburg family held significant banking and policy roles in Europe and the United States during the development of modern finance.
historicalArchitects.presentAssessment: Historical access is relevant to institutional history, but does not establish hereditary present-day control of the Federal Reserve or international banking.

historicalArchitects.name: Medici and Fugger houses
historicalArchitects.documentedHistory: These families illustrate pre-modern combinations of banking, sovereign finance, office, patronage and dynastic power that helped shape later financial and political institutions.
historicalArchitects.presentAssessment: They are historical models, not current power holders. Their value is explanatory: durable power can be built by controlling credit, appointments, information and succession before modern bureaucratic states exist.

structureAccessMatrix.structure: US dollar monetary and sanctions system
formalControllers: Courts and executive authorities within defined powers
structureAccessMatrix.familyAccess: No family has documented legal control. Families may gain access through elected office, regulated financial institutions, advisory networks, donations, ownership or professional relationships, but these routes are fragmented and contestable.

Elite family background may affect informal networks, but the system is formally party-institutional rather than a legally hereditary family structure. Claims about specific families require high-grade evidence.

Private families may gain contractor, donor, advisory or social access. No family has demonstrated ownership of the system; authority is divided by law, budget, classification and institutional command.
Families can influence companies, lobbying, foundations or political networks, but no hereditary family control is established over the EU or Eurosystem.
Founder families or trusts may retain voting control in specific companies. This grants company-level power, not ownership of the entire compute ecosystem.

structureAccessMatrix.structure: Global payment, messaging, settlement and custody rails
structureAccessMatrix.familyAccess: Banking families may have historical or firm-level access, but modern rails are multi-institutional. A claim of family command requires documented voting, appointment or contractual authority.
Founding families can matter inside individual firms, but state export controls, technical expertise and interdependent supply chains prevent simple family ownership of the whole system.
Professional and financial networks can shape consultation, but family control is not established. Standards depend on member-state adoption.

formalControllers: Management and staff within the Articles of Agreement
structureAccessMatrix.familyAccess: Families may influence member governments or financial advisers, but no family owns or legally controls the IMF.
Private investment families and family offices can control large pools, but the wider system is dispersed across fiduciaries, institutions and beneficiaries.
